title: GIAC GPEN
summary: The GIAC Penetration Tester certification, exam code GPEN, is an offensive security credential from GIAC, the certification body of the SANS Institute. It suits penetration testers, red team operators and security consultants who already run authorised assessments against networks and hosts. Passing it shows an employer that you can scope an engagement, perform reconnaissance, exploit weaknesses in network services and operating systems, raise your privileges and move carefully through a target environment without breaking it. The exam is proctored and mixes multiple choice questions with performance based items where you carry out tasks in a live environment, and GIAC allows a printed index that you build yourself. A pass is valid for several years and is renewed through continuing education credits. It leads to roles such as penetration tester, red team operator, security consultant or vulnerability assessment analyst. GIAC updates its outlines periodically, so the domain list below follows the published outline and you should confirm the current version before you book. This is an independent study guide and it is not approved or sponsored by GIAC or SANS.

beginner.definition: This is a certification from GIAC about testing how secure a network really is. A penetration tester is a person who is paid to attack systems with permission. The tester looks for weak points and reports them so the owners can fix them. The exam checks that you can do this work in a careful and organised way.
beginner.whyItMatters: Organisations need proof that their defences work, and a human tester provides that proof. This certificate shows employers that you can act like a real attacker while staying inside the rules of the engagement. It supports consultant, tester and red team roles, which often pay well. It also proves you understand both the technical attack and the reporting that follows. For a career move into offensive security, it is a recognised step.
howItWorks: Build a lab with virtual machines and an isolated network that you own and control.
Learn the legal side first, including written permission, scope and rules of engagement.
Study reconnaissance, scanning and service identification until the tools feel familiar.
Practise exploitation and privilege escalation on purpose built vulnerable machines.
Write a short report for every lab exercise, because findings must be explained clearly.
Prepare a printed index and take the official practice test before booking the exam.
beginner.example: Imagine a company hires you to test the security of one office network. Before you touch anything, you agree in writing which addresses you may test and which you must avoid, because the neighbouring company shares the same building. You then map the network, find an old service, gain a foothold and record every step with the time it happened. At the end you hand over a report that a manager can read and that engineers can act on. The exam tests both the attack and the discipline around it.
takeaways: Permission comes first, so always confirm the scope and rules of engagement in writing.
Lab practice matters more than reading, because the exam includes hands on tasks.
Keep a record of every command you use, since reporting is part of the job.

objectives: Explain the legal and ethical rules that govern an authorised penetration test.
Plan an engagement and define its scope, targets and limits.
Gather information about a target using passive and active techniques.
Exploit known weaknesses in network services and operating systems.
Escalate privileges and move between hosts after an initial foothold.
Report findings with clear evidence and practical fixes.

chapters.title: Network essentials and defence in depth
objectives: Describe how the main network protocols carry data between systems.
Explain how layered defences slow down or stop an attacker.
Read packet captures to understand what happened on a network.
Identify the controls a defender uses to limit an attack.
Recognise how the internet is named, addressed and routed.

chapters.title: Planning and scoping a penetration test
objectives: Agree a written scope that names the systems you may test and those you must avoid.
Set rules of engagement for timing, noise level and emergency contacts.
Identify the legal limits that apply in the relevant jurisdiction.
Choose a testing approach that matches the client goal.
Plan how evidence will be stored and how the report will be delivered.

chapters.title: Information gathering and reconnaissance
objectives: Collect public information about an organisation without alerting it.
Enumerate hosts, open ports and running services on a target network.
Fingerprint operating systems and applications from their responses.
Map the results into a picture of the attack surface.
Record your discoveries in a form you can quote in the final report.

chapters.title: Exploitation of network services and systems
objectives: Match a discovered service to a suitable exploit safely.
Exploit common weaknesses in network services and web interfaces.
Attack authentication mechanisms to recover or reuse credentials.
Assess the risk of an exploit before you run it against a live target.
Document what you did, when you did it and what the target showed.

chapters.title: Privilege escalation, lateral movement and reporting
objectives: Escalate privileges on a compromised host using misconfigurations.
Reuse recovered credentials to reach further systems inside the network.
Collect the evidence needed to prove each finding to the client.
Rate findings by severity using a recognised scoring method.
Write practical recommendations that the client can implement.
